author: Origen of Alexandria
occasion: The surviving fragment addresses a difficulty raised by the book of Ruth: how Ruth the Moabite could enter the assembly of God despite the law's prohibition.
argument: Origen interprets Ruth as a type of the Gentiles, since she left her ancestral ways and was joined to the Israelite way of life. He raises the legal problem that the law forbids a Moabite from entering the assembly of God, yet Ruth the Moabite entered. He proposes to resolve this by applying the principle that the law is not laid down for the righteous but for the lawless and disobedient.

outline.move: The whole surviving fragment states that Ruth is a type of the Gentiles, poses the question of how she could enter God's assembly despite the law against Moabites, and proposes to use the text that the law is not for the righteous; the fragment breaks off with the quotation itself.

cast.name: Ruth
cast.who: The Moabite woman whose name is given to the second woman in the biblical book; interpreted as a type of the Gentiles.

voices.speaker: Pauline epistle (1 Timothy 1:9) quoted as authoritative text
voices.how_marked: Introduced by χρῆσαι τῷ ("to use/apply the [saying] that...") and given as a quotation. The dative article τῷ is not the standard quotation formula; the key marker is χρῆσαι (to use/apply), indicating Origen's hermeneutical application of the text.

key_terms.sense: A figure or pattern that points forward to a later reality; here Ruth as a type of the Gentiles.
The assembly or congregation of God, the covenant community of Israel.
A Moabite, a member of the people descended from Lot, excluded from Israel's assembly by the law.
The righteous person, for whom the law is not imposed as a constraint.
The law of Moses, specifically the legal prohibition against Moabites entering the assembly.

scripture: The fragment quotes a New Testament text (1 Timothy 1:9) in Greek. Biblical books should be cited by their standard English names; the book under discussion is Ruth.
uncertain: The original extent and structure of Origen's work on Ruth are unknown; only this fragment survives.
The exact wording of the biblical text Origen used for the prohibition against Moabites is not quoted in the fragment.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the fragment breaks off with the quotation itself
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ τοῦτο ζητῶν χρῆσαι τῷ· "∆ικαίω δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις."
_unresolved_facts.fix: the fragment ends with the quotation, but the quotation is complete (the full verse from 1 Timothy 1:9 is given), not a breaking-off mid-quotation

_unresolved_facts.claim: The dative article τῷ is not the standard quotation formula
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: χρῆσαι τῷ· "∆ικαίω δὲ νόμος οὐ κεῖται, ἀλλὰ ἀδίκοις καὶ ἀνυποτάκτοις."
_unresolved_facts.fix: τῷ here is the standard demonstrative article introducing a quotation ("to use that [saying]:..."), a common construction with χρῆσαι/χρήσασθαι meaning "to use/apply the [text] that..."
the source does not identify the quotation as from 1 Timothy; this is modern scholarly identification
